activities.anchor: The boring rules are the ones with the highest stakes.
activities.caption: bet before you read on — what one lapse costs
activities.name: kitchStakesPredict

config.q: No diner ever praises the sanitised cutting board. What does a single lapse cost?
choices: One bout of food poisoning can close the restaurant, wreck its reputation — and in the worst cases kill
A late dish loses a tip
A slightly slower service that evening
config.why: Invisible when done well and catastrophic when skipped — grammar is like that.

activities.caption: the strict hierarchy — file each habit
activities.name: kitchHierarchySort

config.prompt: Sanitation, safety or speed? File each habit:

items.label: the cutting board sanitised between raw chicken and the salad
mise en place staging saves minutes at service
handwashing: at least 20 seconds with soap
sharpen weekly so cuts need less force

config.why: A fast cook who cross-contaminates is not a good cook; slowness can be trained out — the order cannot change.

activities.anchor: Bacterial growth is exponential, not linear
activities.caption: call the population after one shift
activities.name: kitchGrowthEst

config.prompt: Starting from a single cell in ideal conditions, how many after 210 minutes of doubling every 20 minutes?
config.why: The four-hour cumulative budget for TCS foods exists because the count multiplies, not adds.
config.context: Delivery, storage, prep and service all share that budget — the clock never resets.

activities.anchor: using shallow pans, ice baths or ice wands
activities.caption: stage one of the two-stage cool
activities.name: kitchCoolPlace

config.prompt: The first stage of stock cooling: from 60 °C down to what temperature, within two hours?
config.why: Then down to 5 °C within four more — a full 20-litre pot can sit mid-zone for half a day, its centre still 30 °C at midnight, right where Clostridium perfringens thrives.

activities.anchor: A surface can look spotless and still be a biohazard
activities.caption: pair each rule with the transfer it stops
activities.name: kitchCrossMatch

config.prompt: Pair each rule with what it stops:

pairs.left: raw poultry stores below ready-to-eat items
pairs.right: drips falling onto food that will not be cooked again

pairs.left: 20 seconds of soap after raw proteins, money or rubbish
heat sanitising — 77 °C for 30 seconds — or chlorine at 50–100 ppm
pairs.right: microorganisms above safe levels, on a wash-first surface

config.why: Cleaning removes visible soil; sanitising makes it food-safe — in that order.

activities.anchor: In a hospital kitchen, for example, cooking chicken to an internal 74 °C for at least 15 seconds is a CCP
activities.caption: HACCP's seven principles, in order
activities.name: kitchHaccpOrder

config.prompt: HACCP's seven principles — put them in order:
items: Establish corrective actions when a limit is breached
config.why: Born keeping astronauts' food safe — the last reliable point where pathogens are destroyed gets probed, logged and enforced.

activities.anchor: The clock and the thermometer, not the nose, are the safety instruments.
activities.caption: true or false — can you trust your senses?
activities.name: kitchSpoilJudge

statements.s: You can tell food has gone bad by looking at it or smelling it.
statements.why: The bacteria that make you sick usually produce no smell, no slime, no colour change — those signals come from spoilage organisms, a different and relatively harmless crowd.

statements.s: Rice left out overnight can look and smell fine while carrying enough Bacillus cereus toxin to cause vomiting.
Spoilage organisms are the same crowd as the bacteria that cause illness.
statements.why: The visible, smelly signals come from the relatively harmless spoilage side.

statements.s: Time and temperature monitoring beats sniffing, every time.
statements.why: Exponential growth hides in a perfectly presentable pot.

activities.anchor: and never gesture or talk while holding one
activities.caption: the falling knife — walk the moment
activities.name: kitchKnifeBranch

config.root: Mid-service, the knife starts to fall off the bench.

choices.label: Step back and let it land
choices.feedback: Feet back, fingers clear — the grab reflex is what costs hands.

choices.label: Catch it mid-air
choices.feedback: That reflex is precisely how the worst hand injuries happen.

catch.text: Bandages and a lesson: let it fall — and never go fishing for a blade under foam.

step.text: It lands. The rest of the discipline?

choices.label: Carry tip down, edge away; cut on a board, never metal; cut away from the body
choices.feedback: The trade's everyday injury has standing rules — and a sharp blade needs less force, so it slips far less.

choices.label: Soak it in the sink until the rush is over
choices.feedback: A hidden blade under foam is a trap — never leave a knife in soapy water, never reach in to search.

sink.text: The sink is the trap the rules warn about — retrieve with the handle visible, or do not soak it at all.

rules.text: Right knife for the job, board always, away from the body, tip down in transit — and no chatting mid-cut.

config.why: Cuts are the trade's everyday injury — and the rules are specific because they are predictable.
